blocks.text: When a car maker says a 2.0 litre engine produces 110 kW, the number is not the power the gas does on the pistons; it is the power available at the flywheel after the engine has paid for its own friction and pumping. Three simple measurements, pressure in the cylinders, torque on a dynamometer and fuel flow, allow every performance figure of the engine to be computed. This unit shows how.

blocks.markdown: A reciprocating engine converts the heat of burning fuel into work on the pistons, and then into work at the crankshaft. Each cycle, the gas in the cylinder does **indicated work**, the area of the pressure-volume diagram. The shaft delivers less, because the engine must overcome friction, drive pumps and valves, and pump gas in and out. We separate these effects with three powers and three efficiency-like measures.

blocks.title: Indicated power, brake power and mean effective pressure
blocks.text: The **indicated mean effective pressure** (imep) is the constant pressure that, acting on the piston over the swept volume, would do the same work as the real cycle: $W_i=\text{imep}\times V_d$ per cylinder per cycle, where $V_d$ is the swept (displacement) volume. The **indicated power** $P_i$ is the work per cycle times cycles per second. The **brake power** $P_b$ is that measured at the output shaft with a dynamometer: $P_b=2\pi NT/60$ for shaft speed $N$ (rpm) and torque $T$ (N m). **Friction power** is $P_f=P_i-P_b$.

blocks.caption: Indicated power (V_d is the total displacement; n_R = 2 revolutions per cycle for a four-stroke, 1 for a two-stroke), brake power and mechanical efficiency

blocks.title: Indicated power of a four-cylinder engine
blocks.prompt: A four-cylinder, four-stroke engine has total displacement 2 L (0.002 m$^3$) and an indicated mean effective pressure of 1.05 MPa at 3000 rpm. Find the indicated power.

steps.text: A four-stroke engine completes one cycle every two revolutions, so $n_R=2$ revolutions per cycle.
Work per cycle for the whole engine is imep times the total displacement.
Power is work per cycle times cycles per second.

blocks.answer: The indicated power is about 52.5 kW.

blocks.title: Brake power, mechanical efficiency and bsfc
blocks.prompt: The same engine is tested on a dynamometer at 3000 rpm. The measured torque is 120 N m and the fuel (gasoline, typical $LHV=44$ MJ/kg) flow is 0.0027 kg/s. Find the brake power, mechanical efficiency, friction power, brake specific fuel consumption, brake thermal efficiency and brake mean effective pressure.

steps.text: Brake power from torque and speed.
Mechanical efficiency and friction power, using the indicated power above.
Brake specific fuel consumption is fuel mass flow per unit brake power.
Brake thermal efficiency: brake power over fuel energy rate.

blocks.answer: $P_b\approx37.7$ kW, $\eta_m\approx0.718$, $P_f\approx14.8$ kW, bsfc $\approx258$ g/kWh, $\eta_b\approx0.317$ and bmep $\approx0.754$ MPa.

rows: Fraction not lost to friction and pumping; typically 0.8 to 0.9 near full load (typical)
Torque per unit displacement; compares engines of different size
Fuel per unit energy delivered; lower is better, typically 250 to 350 g/kWh for gasoline engines (typical)
Fraction of fuel energy delivered to the shaft
blocks.caption: Indicated and brake performance measures

blocks.markdown: **How the measures behave.** Friction power rises with speed, and is nearly independent of load. At light load the indicated power is small, so $P_f/P_i$ is large and $\eta_m$ falls, even to zero at idle when $P_b=0$. Because bmep and bsfc are normalised by displacement and brake power respectively, they allow engines of different size and speed to be compared: bmep is a measure of how hard the engine works its displacement, and bsfc of how well it uses fuel.

items: Convert speed to rad/s or use $N/60$; keep torque in N m to get brake power in W.
For indicated power, remember $n_R=2$ for four-stroke engines (one power stroke every two revolutions) and $n_R=1$ for two-stroke engines.
Obtain friction power as $P_i-P_b$ (or from a motoring test, or by extrapolating fuel use against load to zero brake power, the Willans line).
Convert bsfc to brake thermal efficiency with $\eta_b=3.6/(bsfc\cdot LHV)$ when bsfc is in kg/kWh and $LHV$ in MJ/kg.

blocks.title: Check the revolutions per cycle
blocks.text: Using $n_R=1$ for a four-stroke engine overstates the indicated power by a factor of two. Always confirm the engine type. Also check that displacement is total (all cylinders) when using imep with total $V_d$, or per cylinder with the per-cylinder displacement and then multiplying by the number of cylinders.

points: Indicated power $P_i=\text{imep}\,V_dN/(60n_R)$; brake power $P_b=2\pi NT/60$; mechanical efficiency $\eta_m=P_b/P_i$.
Brake specific fuel consumption $bsfc=\dot m_f/P_b$ and brake thermal efficiency $\eta_b=3.6/(bsfc\cdot LHV)$ (kg/kWh, MJ/kg).
Mechanical efficiency falls at light load, since friction power is almost independent of load.

questions.stem: Two engines have the same displacement, speed and imep. One is a four-stroke, the other a two-stroke. The indicated power of the two-stroke is, in the ideal case:

options.text: twice that of the four-stroke, because it has a power stroke every revolution
half that of the four-stroke, because it has fewer strokes per cycle
the same as the four-stroke, because imep and displacement set the work
four times that of the four-stroke, because it has half as many strokes

questions.correctOptionText: twice that of the four-stroke, because it has a power stroke every revolution

distractorRationale.a: Correct: n_R is 1 rather than 2, giving twice as many power strokes.
distractorRationale.b: The two-stroke has a power stroke on every revolution rather than every second one.
distractorRationale.c: The number of cycles per second also matters: the power is the work per cycle times cycles per second.
distractorRationale.d: The ratio of power strokes is two, not four.

questions.explanation: Power is work per cycle times cycles per second, $P_i=\text{imep}\,V_dN/(60n_R)$. The two-stroke has $n_R=1$ and the four-stroke $n_R=2$, so the two-stroke's indicated power is twice as large.

questions.stem: An engine develops an indicated power of 75 kW and delivers a brake power of 60 kW at the flywheel. Its mechanical efficiency is:

distractorRationale.a: Inverts the ratio (indicated over brake), giving a value above one.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: brake power divided by indicated power.
distractorRationale.c: Takes the friction fraction, the complement of the mechanical efficiency.
distractorRationale.d: Takes the brake power as a fraction of 100 kW without basis in the data.

questions.explanation: Mechanical efficiency is brake power over indicated power: $60/75=0.80$. The friction and pumping power is the other 15 kW, which is 20 per cent of the indicated power.

questions.stem: A four-stroke engine with a total displacement of 1.6 L runs at 4500 rpm with an imep of 0.90 MPa. The indicated power is closest to:

distractorRationale.a: Uses one cycle per revolution, which would be correct for a two-stroke engine.
distractorRationale.b: Divides by an extra factor of 60 from mis-handling the speed conversion.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: work per cycle times 37.5 cycles per second.
distractorRationale.d: Multiplies by the displacement in litres a second time.

questions.explanation: Work per cycle is $0.90\times10^{6}\times0.0016=1440$ J. Cycles per second are $4500/120=37.5$, so $P_i=1440\times37.5=54000$ W.

questions.stem: Test A gives a bsfc of 240 g/kWh and test B a bsfc of 300 g/kWh on the same engine and fuel. Compared with A, the brake thermal efficiency in B is:

options.text: the same, because the fuel is the same

distractorRationale.a: The efficiency is inversely proportional to bsfc, so a larger bsfc means a lower efficiency.
distractorRationale.b: The efficiency depends on how much fuel is used per unit of brake energy.
distractorRationale.c: Squares the ratio; the relation is inverse-proportional, not quadratic.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: efficiency scales as the reciprocal of bsfc.

questions.explanation: Since $\eta_b=3.6/(bsfc\cdot LHV)$, efficiency is inversely proportional to bsfc: $\eta_B/\eta_A=240/300=0.80$. More fuel per kWh means less of its energy reaches the shaft.

questions.stem: An engine is throttled to light load at constant speed. Which statement about its mechanical efficiency is correct?

options.text: It falls, because the friction power stays almost constant while the indicated power drops
It rises, because less fuel is burned
It is unchanged, because friction is a fixed fraction of brake power

questions.correctOptionText: It falls, because the friction power stays almost constant while the indicated power drops

distractorRationale.a: Correct: constant friction power against falling indicated power.
distractorRationale.b: Friction does not fall in proportion to the fuel, so the fraction lost rises.
distractorRationale.c: Friction is nearly independent of load, not proportional to brake power.
distractorRationale.d: At idle the brake power is zero, so the mechanical efficiency is zero.

questions.explanation: With $P_f$ nearly constant at a given speed, $\eta_m=1-P_f/P_i$ decreases as $P_i$ falls. At idle all of the indicated power just supplies the friction, so $\eta_m=0$.

questions.stem: A dynamometer measures a torque of 210 N m on an engine running at 2400 rpm. Find the brake power in kW.
questions.explanation: Brake power is $P_b=2\pi NT/60=2\pi\times2400\times210/60=52779$ W, which is 52.78 kW.

questions.stem: An engine delivers a brake power of 60.0 kW while burning 0.0042 kg/s of fuel. Find the brake specific fuel consumption in g/kWh.
questions.explanation: Fuel per hour is $0.0042\times3600=15.12$ kg/h. Dividing by 60.0 kW gives $0.252$ kg/kWh, which is 252 g/kWh.

questions.stem: A six-cylinder four-stroke diesel engine of total displacement 7.0 L runs at 2200 rpm with an imep of 0.95 MPa and a mechanical efficiency of 0.84. Find its brake power in kW.
questions.explanation: The indicated power is $0.95\times10^{6}\times0.007\times2200/120=1.2192\times10^{5}$ W, i.e. 121.9 kW. The brake power is $\eta_mP_i=0.84\times121.9=102.4$ kW.

questions.stem: Describe two methods of finding the mechanical efficiency of a multi-cylinder engine and the main contributions to the friction power. Explain why mechanical efficiency drops at light load and at high speed.
markingGuide: Method 1: measure indicated power from a cylinder pressure transducer and brake power from the dynamometer, then eta_m = P_b/P_i

Method 2: motoring test (drive the engine with the dynamometer at the same speed and measure the power absorbed to give friction power) or Willans line (fuel flow against brake power extrapolated to zero power)
Friction contributions: piston and ring friction, bearings, valve train, and auxiliaries such as oil and water pumps
Pumping losses (intake throttling) are often included in friction power
At light load P_i falls while P_f is almost constant so eta_m = 1 - P_f/P_i falls
Friction rises with speed (rubbing speeds and pumping) so eta_m falls at high speed
questions.explanation: Mechanical efficiency is the ratio of brake to indicated power, so it can be measured directly if both are known, or the friction power can be found from a motoring test. Friction power is nearly load-independent and increases with speed, so the efficiency falls at low load and high speed.

questions.stem: Derive the expression for the indicated power of a four-stroke engine in terms of imep, displacement and speed. Then explain how brake specific fuel consumption relates to brake thermal efficiency, and why bmep is useful for comparing engines.
markingGuide: Work per cycle for the whole engine W_i = imep x V_d (imep defined as constant pressure equivalent to cycle work over swept volume)
Four-stroke: one cycle every two revolutions, so cycles per second = N/(60 x 2)
P_i = imep V_d N / 120 for the four-stroke
bsfc = m_f/P_b in kg/kWh; eta_b = P_b/(m_f LHV) = 3.6/(bsfc LHV)
Lower bsfc means higher efficiency (inverse relation)
bmep = P_b 120/(V_d N) is torque per unit displacement, independent of size and speed, so it indicates how well the displacement is used and permits comparison of engines
questions.explanation: The cycle work is the imep times the swept volume, and a four-stroke engine completes $N/120$ cycles per second. Since fuel energy rate is $\dot m_fLHV$ and brake power is $P_b$, the efficiency is inversely proportional to bsfc. The bmep expresses torque per unit displacement, so it measures how hard an engine works its displacement irrespective of size.
